extracted.intended_audience: journalism students and newspaper reporters covering meetings, hearings, and investigations
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing news stories about official meetings, legislative sessions, conventions, and investigative/hearing proceedings, focusing on what to include, how to treat testimony, tone, and public-interest obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select significant parts of proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: The parts of the proceedings that are of general interest and significance make up the contents of such stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters should identify and present the elements of meetings or hearings that matter to the public rather than attempting a blow-by-blow account. (References: “The purely informative type of story is the common form for reporting meetings... The parts of the proceedings that are of general interest and significance make up the contents of such stories.”)

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose — accuracy and completeness proportionate to significance
rubrics_metrics.description: To give the facts accurately and as completely as their significance warrants should be the first aim in reporting proceedings of official bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accuracy and completeness are primary; the desire to accomplish an end does not justify distortion or suppression. Even constructive aims (exposing sinister influences) do not legitimize misrepresenting facts. (Text: “The desire to accomplish some end... does not justify distortion or suppression of the news... distortion or suppression of facts in order to make out a stronger case is not legitimate.”)

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid partisan misrepresentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not misrepresent public matters to create opinion favorable to a political cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Politically partisan stories that misrepresent official proceedings hurt the paper’s reputation and public trust in newspapers in general. Maintain impartiality in reports of representative public bodies and political meetings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextualize significance for readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Show the significance of acts of representative public bodies in relation to home and business interests of the reader, and to the welfare of the community, state, and nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why proceedings matter to ordinary readers to foster intelligent interest in government, which is essential to democracy. (Text: “Much more effort should be made by newspapers... to show the significance of acts of representative public bodies, in relation not only to the home and business interests of the individual reader, but to the welfare of the community, the state, and the nation.”)

rubrics_metrics.name: Make dry proceedings interesting through explanation and description
rubrics_metrics.description: To make interesting what is often considered dry and unattractive in proceedings is the chief problem in writing news stories concerning them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use simple, clear explanation of the meaning of significant parts, lively accounts of debate on measures, and vivid description of persons and scenes to add interest. Use human-interest or humorous elements legitimately when fitting. (Text examples: “Simple, clear explanation... lively accounts of debate... vivid description of persons and scenes.”)

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not overplay insignificant incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Too often insignificant incidents of casual interest are played up as features of meetings of importance to the subordination or even to the exclusion of matters of vital concern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid emphasizing trivial or colorful side incidents at the expense of the vital issues before the body; keep focus on what materially matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate tone: informative vs. human-interest/humorous
rubrics_metrics.description: Some meetings lend themselves to humorous treatment, and when the news interest in them is slight, such stories about them constitute typical human interest stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide tone based on the meeting's news value: use a purely informative form for important proceedings; deploy human-interest or humorous angles only when the substantive news interest is limited and such treatment is legitimate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle testimony like court reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Testimony in investigations and hearings is sometimes like that in court trials; the questions and the answers in these proceedings are handled like those in court stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters should treat witness testimony with the same techniques used in court reporting — focusing on striking, significant exchanges, accurately reporting questions and answers, and noting dramatic phases when present. Examples in the chapter illustrate testimony-driven scenes (e.g., congressional and commission testimony).

rubrics_metrics.name: Select vital matters, present concisely, and condense routine details
rubrics_metrics.description: To select the vital matters, to present them concisely, and to condense routine but necessary details into the smallest possible compass in stories of this class, require effort and skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize and compress: give the essential facts up front, summarize procedural or routine items tersely, and reserve space for the most significant developments or testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize investigations/hearings as often quasi-judicial
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigations and hearings as conducted by committees of legislative bodies are also placed in this class, although they are often more like judicial proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat such proceedings with awareness of legal/judicial forms (formal testimony, procedural motions, counsel statements) and adapt reporting practices accordingly (e.g., identifying counsel, noting filings and formal charges).
